newsitem.title: USA: Security group sounds alarm about computer crime.
newsitem.headline: Security group sounds alarm about computer crime.

text.p: A computer security group sounded an alarm about computer crime on Thursday after U.S. companies and other organisations it surveyed reported losing $100 million due to high-tech crime.

Three-quarters of the 563 U.S. corporations, government agencies, financial institutions and universities which responded to the survey by the Computer Security Institute reported suffering financial losses in the last 12 months due to computer security breaches.
The breaches ranged from computer viruses and laptop theft to financial fraud, theft of proprietary information and sabotage.

Losses suffered by the 249 organisations that were able to estimate them totalled $100 million in the last year, the Computer Security Institute, a San Francisco-based association of information security professionals, said.
Institute director Patrice Rapalus said the survey's findings about financial losses due to security breaches "should sound the alarm for corporations and government agencies."
She said the level of awareness of computer crime had risen slightly since the institute carried out its first survey last year but most organisations still were not doing enough to counter it.
Richard Power, a spokesman for the institute, said it was likely that computer crime cost billions of dollars each year in the United States, although this was not based on data from the survey.
Power said there was a need for more information security staff, more security training for computer network administrators and for greater cooperation between the private sector and law enforcement.

The institute's first computer crime survey last May did not estimate financial losses. Questions for the survey were provided by the San Francisco office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation's International Computer Crime Squad.

The organisations reported $24.9 million in losses from financial fraud, $22.7 million due to telecommunications fraud, $21 million from theft of proprietary information, $4.3 million from sabotage of data or networks, $12.5 million from computer viruses and $6.1 million from theft of laptop computers, the institute said.

The number of organisations that suffered an intrusion or other unauthorised use of computer systems in the last 12 months rose to 49 percent in the latest survey from 42 percent in the 1996 survey, the institute said.

However, only 17 percent of respondents who suffered computer intrusions reported them to law enforcement, the survey found. Fear of negative publicity was a key reason organisations did not report them, it found.

The number of organisations that perceived their Internet connection as a frequent point of attack rose to 47 percent from 37 percent last year, it added. More than half perceived internal systems as a frequent point of attack, it said.

More than 80 percent of respondents perceived disgruntled employees as a likely source of attack of their computer systems and more than 70 percent saw hackers as a likely source, the survey found. U.S. and foreign corporate competitors and foreign governments were perceived as a likely source of attack by smaller numbers of respondents.

In the 1996 survey, over 70 percent of respondents said their organisations did not have a "warning" banner on their systems stating that computing activities may be monitored. That number fell this year to less than half. The number of respondents without a policy for preserving evidence for criminal or civil proceedings fell to 55 from 60 percent.
